title: TCP Reliability & Flow Control
summary: How TCP guarantees ordered, lossless delivery via sequence numbers and retransmission, and paces a fast sender against a slow receiver.

slides.markdown:
TCP numbers every byte in the stream, not every segment. An **ACK** doesn't mean "I got segment 5" — it means "I've received everything up through byte N, send me byte N+1 next."

This byte-level, cumulative accounting is what lets TCP detect a gap (a missing range of bytes) and know exactly where to resume, even if segments arrive out of order or get split differently than they were sent.

TCP has two ways to notice loss:

- **Timeout-based:** if no ACK arrives within the retransmission timeout (RTO, adaptively computed from measured RTT), resend the unacknowledged segment.
- **Fast retransmit:** if the sender sees **three duplicate ACKs** in a row (the receiver repeating "still waiting for byte N"), it resends immediately — without waiting for the timeout.

Fast retransmit exists because timeouts are conservative and slow; duplicate ACKs are a much quicker loss signal available most of the time.

TCP doesn't send one segment and wait for its ACK — that would waste the whole round trip. Instead it keeps a **window** of unacknowledged bytes in flight simultaneously, sliding forward as ACKs confirm delivery.

A bigger window means more data in flight per round trip, which is exactly why window size drives achievable throughput on a high-latency link.

assets.alt: TCP sliding window advancing as ACKs arrive

slides.markdown:
**Flow control** stops a fast sender from overrunning a slow receiver's buffer. The receiver advertises a **receive window (rwnd)** in every ACK — "I have room for this many more bytes" — and the sender is not allowed to have more unacknowledged data in flight than that.

If the receiver's application is slow to read (rwnd shrinks toward zero), the sender throttles down, even if the network itself has plenty of spare capacity.

As ACKs arrive confirming earlier bytes, the window's left edge advances (those bytes are done) and the right edge advances too (more bytes are now allowed to be sent) — hence "sliding."

Bytes already acknowledged fall out of the window entirely; the sender never has to think about them again.

assets.alt: Sliding window advancing left and right edges as ACKs confirm bytes

slides.markdown:
Plain cumulative ACKs only ever say "I have everything up to byte N" — if bytes N+1 through N+3000 arrive but N+3001 through N+4000 is lost and then N+4001 onward arrives, a cumulative ACK still just says N, hiding the fact that most of the later data actually arrived.

**SACK (Selective Acknowledgment)** fixes this: the receiver explicitly lists the *out-of-order blocks* it already has, so the sender retransmits only the actual gap instead of everything after it.

IP makes no ordering promise, so segments can legitimately arrive at the receiver in a different order than they were sent (different routing paths, retransmissions, reordering in the network).

TCP buffers out-of-order segments on arrival rather than discarding them, and reassembles the byte stream once the missing piece fills the gap — the application only ever sees a clean, ordered stream.

**Nagle's algorithm** batches small outgoing writes into fewer segments instead of sending each as its own tiny, overhead-heavy packet. **Delayed ACK** mirrors this on the receiver — waiting briefly to piggyback an ACK on outgoing data instead of sending it alone.

**The trap:** combine both defaults and a request-response protocol can stall ~40ms per round trip — Nagle waits for an ACK before sending the next chunk, while the peer's delayed-ACK timer waits to piggyback that very ACK. Latency-sensitive apps disable Nagle (`TCP_NODELAY`) for this reason.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: flow control vs congestion control
slides.markdown:
| | Flow control | Congestion control |
|---|---|---|
| Protects | The receiver's buffer | The network's shared capacity |
| Signal used | Advertised receive window (rwnd) | Inferred loss/delay, congestion window (cwnd) |
| Who sets the limit | The receiver | The sender, inferring from the path |

How to decide which is limiting throughput: check whether rwnd or cwnd is the smaller value — TCP always sends at most `min(rwnd, cwnd)`. See [TCP Congestion Control](tcp-congestion-control) for the other half.

**Wrong belief:** "TCP guarantees my data arrives quickly and in order, so it's the fast, safe choice."

**Why it's wrong:** TCP guarantees **order and eventual delivery**, not low latency. Retransmission waits, window limits, Nagle/delayed-ACK interaction, and congestion backoff all add real delay — that's the price of the guarantee, not a bug.

**Correct model:** reliability and speed are different axes. That's why latency-sensitive, loss-tolerant apps (voice, live video, gaming) often choose UDP and build only the reliability they actually need.
